chapter: Basie and life on the road
title: White women and danger at dances
summary: Flirting by white women at southern dances; Lee Allen whipped in New Orleans.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Now, were there times when you had, when you all played, say for a white audience? Mm-hmm. Where, where, there were white women? Mm-hmm. Was that a problem?

Yeah, probably, especially down south, because those women are coming up there and start flirting with you and pulling on you, and your husband's sitting down there looking at you like he wanted to kill you. And you try, oh, you try to be nice, yeah, yeah, well, yeah, well, look, come on, come here, come here, and man, they'd throw their arms around you and hug you. Like I played in Buckaloosa, you know what Buckaloosa is? Just before I went away, before I started traveling, I played in Buck, we used to play Buckaloosa every night, and man, they had some white people out there who were mean. But they liked the band. If you liked the band, and you don't mess around with those white women, you're all right with them. So there's a guy playing saxophone with the band. He was there playing, a woman at the dance, and she winked at him. And just when he winked back at her, her husband turned around and he saw him wink at her. And man, this guy had to wink all night to make the guy think that something was wrong with his eye. He took his handkerchief about it and started rubbing his eyes. And I said, what's wrong man? I was winging this woman her husband, caught me.
Well, did anything ever bad happen to anybody? Yeah, Lee Allen.

You know Lee Allen or something? Yeah. Man, he whipped Lee right in New Orleans. When was this? This was back then, the forties. Man, he was, but he was, but you know, are you from here? Yeah, I'm from here. Man, look, at one time they were hard on black men for messing around white women. But there was always the woman who hit on a man.

So this woman wrote Lee a note and gave it to the white bartender to pass it over to Lee. Because the band was playing on, this was on Burbin and I, the band's team was back, elevated, behind the bar. And he was getting on the other side. So this woman gave this note to him to read. I mean, for him to give to Lee. Lee read the note and answered it. And gave it back to this guy, because a guy like Lee. But just when he took, when he got ready to read for it, another guy on other side took the metal out of the guy's hand and read it. And he got his guys together and mainly took me outside and gave him a gun. Now, that happened to me one time, you know, like several times. I'm on the bandstand, you know, like, especially if it's my band. Woman sent a note up there to me. I look at it, say it up. I said, now ladies and gentlemen, we have a request to play for, let me see, hold on. Oh, Mrs. Jones, we have a request to play for Mrs. Jones. She wants to hear start us. So I give everybody in the place, think that was a request that was sent up to me, you know. Right.
And, and so, sometimes something happened that, that they... No, no.
See, a lot of guys would take chances. I didn't want to take, I didn't want to take any chances. Because I have too many, I had too many other women. Mm-hmm.
Sure. So the only things that would happen is you'd get past the note, you wouldn't, but you wouldn't follow through on it.
